What opt did on small problems.

Each story is a real run of opt, written into this page by scripts/gen_stories.py, with what it shows and what it does not. The data are invented and seeded; none of it measures the world. Numbers are rounded to six significant digits; the runs were made on Linux x86-64.

Eight points no line separates

Logistic regression on eight invented points (two features), with a small ridge so the answer is unique and its gradient written out. opt asks the program for the loss and the gradient at a point and runs BFGS.

$ opt minimize --method bfgs --x0 0,0,0 -- python3 examples/train/logistic.py
{"method":"bfgs","x":[2.28644,2.41774,2.04962e-16],"fun":0.230847,"nfev":15,"converged":true}

It converged in 15 evaluations to a loss of 0.230847. A Newton solve of the same loss, written separately (examples/train/reference.py), gives 0.230847: they differ by 7.6e-13. The largest gradient component at the answer is 3.0e-07.

Shows: BFGS on a convex problem reaching the answer an independent method reaches, with the evaluations counted. Does not show: that this is the right model, only the minimum of this loss; or any other data.

XOR: converged is not solved

A 2-2-1 sigmoid network (nine parameters) on XOR, cross-entropy loss, backpropagation written by hand. Eight fixed starting points, BFGS from each.

$ opt minimize --method bfgs --x0 <start> -- python3 examples/train/mlp_xor.py
startfinal lossevaluationsconvergedsolved XOR
10.477468yesno
20.477433yesno
30.346648yesno
40.477443yesno
57.739e-0630yesyes
60.477427yesno
70.346649yesno
80.477434yesno

converged was true from 8 of the 8 starts and the network classified all four points from 1. The others stopped at a local minimum, where the gradient is zero and the loss is not.

Shows: that converged means the gradient is small, not that the model is right; a network has local minima that a convex fit does not. Does not show: how often random starts succeed (eight fixed ones are not a sample), or anything about larger networks.

A loss you can only sample

The logistic loss estimated on five of the eight points, drawn from a hash of the point (so a run is reproducible, and the value is noisy). No gradient is printed. SPSA needs two evaluations an iteration whatever the dimension.

$ opt minimize --method spsa --x0 0,0,0 --maxiter 300 -- python3 examples/train/noisy_logistic.py
{"method":"spsa","x":[0.864419,0.176083,-0.140115],"fun":0.591315,"nfev":601,"nit":300,"completed":true}

The fun it prints is one noisy sample. The true loss, computed here from the full data, went from 0.6931 at the start to 0.376 at the answer; the best possible is 0.2308. It moved the right way and had not arrived after 300 iterations (601 evaluations).

Shows: SPSA lowering a noisy loss with no gradient. Does not show: that SPSA converges well on any problem (design.md section 11 says what is and is not claimed).

A loss with corners

A two-unit ReLU network fitted to |x| on nine points. max(0, z) has no derivative at 0, so the program prints a value only, and Nelder-Mead needs nothing more.

$ opt minimize --x0 0.5,0.1,-0.5,0.1,0.8,0.8,0 --maxfev 4000 -- python3 examples/train/relu_fit.py
{"method":"nelder-mead","fun":1.42651e-13,"nfev":2039,"converged":true}

Loss 1.43e-13 after 2039 evaluations, converged: true.

Shows: a derivative-free method on a loss a gradient method cannot take. Does not show: that the simplex finds the global minimum from other starts (one start was run).

Check the gradient before you trust BFGS

examples/train/gradcheck.py compares a program's gradient with central differences at a point. Three versions of the logistic program, checked at (0.3, -0.2, 0.1) and then given to BFGS from the origin; the best possible loss is 0.23085.

versionlargest relative disagreementgradcheckBFGS convergedevaluationsloss reached
the program as it is8.8e-11passesyes150.23085
the bias gradient doubled2.4e-02flags ityes150.23085
the ridge term missing from the gradient3.0e-03flags itno (desired error not necessarily achieved due to precision loss)720.25796

The check flags both wrong versions. BFGS shows only one of them: with the bias gradient doubled, the gradient still vanishes where the true one does (the true bias gradient is zero at the optimum), so BFGS converged to the right answer anyway. With the ridge term missing, the loss and its gradient disagree, the line search fails, and BFGS stops with a loss above the optimum (exit status 1).

Shows: that a wrong gradient can look fine or fail depending on where it is wrong, and that the check finds both. Does not show: that a gradient which passes at one point is right everywhere.

A model whose loss is computed by GPU kernels not run by this page's generator

A least-squares fit whose loss and gradient are computed by cancho-gpu kernels (cancho-gpu run), driven by opt minimize --method bfgs: the objective is a program that calls those kernels twice and prints the loss and the gradient.

$ opt minimize --method bfgs --x0 0,0,0 -- python3 examples/train/lsq_objective.py <cancho-gpu> <checkout>

It converged in 12 evaluations to within 1.1e-5 of the normal-equations solution, at 28 to 36 ms an evaluation over three runs. This story is not run by this page's generator: it needs cancho-gpu's binary. The numbers are those of cancho-gpu's own check (scripts/check_train.py, run.md section 6).

Shows: a kernel as an optimiser's objective. Does not show: anything on a GPU (the device programs do not take input yet), more than 32 parameters (the limit of opt), or a speed claim.
